newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN criticizes Croatia for keeping Serbs out.
newsitem.headline: UN criticizes Croatia for keeping Serbs out.

text.p: Despite public statements to the contrary, Croatia has discouraged Croatian Serbs from returning home and discriminated against those who stayed, the United Nations said.

"A legitimate question may be raised as to whether Croatian Serbs in the region will be able to re-establish the conditions of normal life in the near future," said Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali in a Monday report requested by the Security Council.
"Many Croatian authorities and residents simply do not wish Croatian Serbs to return or, in the cases of Croatia Serbs who remained, do not wish them to stay," he said.
Up to 200,000 Serbs fled when Zagreb troops recaptured the Krajina region in two swift offensives a year ago. Only a few remained in the area, once a stronghold of rebel Serbs.
About 12,000 have been allowed to return but the government's main concern is for thousands of Croat refugees who fled the fighting and need a place to live.

Boutros-Ghali said there were several significant legal developments in the past few months, including adoption of an amnesty law on Sept. 25 and Croatia's admission to the Council of Europe on Nov. 6, which entailed human rights obligations.
He also said that Croatia had made considerable progress in providing humanitarian assistance to many people in need in the former Serb-dominated areas, although discrimination was evident here also.
But Boutros-Ghali said that little progress had been made in allowing Serb civilians to return to their homes.

He said that the situation was especially alarming for the elderly who remained. "The absence of their younger family members will compound the difficulties they will have to face in the coming winter," he said.
Many of those who did return found their homes occupied by Croat refugees and were left with nowhere to live.

Croatia has maintained that crime in the former Serb areas is no higher than in the rest of the country. But the United Nations said many of the incidents, including murder, looting and rape were "specifically motivated by the victims' Croatian Serb origin."

Zagreb also continued to refuse to cooperate fully with the Hague-based U.N. war crimes tribunal or to attempt serious investigations of crimes carried out against Serb civilians during the 1995 offensive, the report said.
